_comment: One file per on-chain service. Related verticals are bundled into one service so they share one registration fee and one container. Member scores: when a member's own polarity matches (or no 'direction' is set) the hub's composite_score is used; when 'direction' differs from the hub's polarity (for example a neutral price series read as cost pressure), the pack scores it from the percentile in that direction. Neutral members without a direction are reported under 'watch', not averaged.
description: Scored US and global macro briefs from official public data (FRED, BLS, BEA, World Bank): economic regime, inflation, labor market, rates and yield curve, bank credit stress, commodities and supply chain, housing, consumer health, and 8-country comparisons of the economy, governance and stability, health systems and education. Each brief is a 0-100 score with label, trend versus the horizon, the inputs that drive it, risk flags, confidence and a citation for every input. Includes a CPI inflation calculator.

verticals.title: US macro regime
verticals.question: Is the US economy strengthening or weakening, and why?

verticals.title: US inflation pulse
verticals.question: Is inflation pressure building or easing?
verticals.note: Higher score means less inflation pressure than usual (all inputs read higher = more inflation = weaker).

verticals.title: US labor market
verticals.question: How strong is the US job market?

verticals.title: US rates and yield curve
verticals.question: Are financial conditions tightening, and is the yield curve inverted?
verticals.note: Higher score means easier conditions: lower policy and Treasury rates than usual and a steeper curve.

verticals.title: US bank credit conditions
verticals.question: Is consumer or bank credit stress rising?
verticals.note: Higher score means healthier credit: deposit and loan growth above usual, delinquencies below.

verticals.title: Commodity and supply chain costs
verticals.question: Are energy, metals and freight adding cost pressure?
verticals.note: Higher score means less cost pressure: energy and industrial metal prices (aluminum, nickel, zinc, iron ore, copper) lower than usual for their trailing history, freight activity healthy. Gold, silver and platinum (World Bank Pink Sheet) are watch items.

verticals.title: Country comparison
verticals.question: How do these economies compare on growth, inflation and jobs?
verticals.note: Annual World Bank data (latest year each country has reported). Country score averages the hub's scores for the directional indicators.

verticals.title: US housing market
verticals.question: Is US housing heating up or cooling down?
verticals.note: Higher score means a hotter market than usual: starts, permits, new-home sales and price growth above their own history, and fewer months of unsold supply.

verticals.title: US consumer health
verticals.question: How strong is the US consumer: spending, income and credit?
verticals.note: Higher score means a stronger consumer than usual: real spending, real income and retail sales growing faster than their own history, card delinquencies lower. Saving rate and consumer credit growth are watch items.

verticals.title: Country governance and stability
verticals.question: How stable and well governed is each of these countries?
verticals.note: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (annual estimates, about -2.5 weak to +2.5 strong). Ranked values compare countries with each other; country score averages the hub's scores, which compare each country with its own history.

verticals.title: Country health systems
verticals.question: How do these countries compare on health outcomes and health spending?
verticals.note: Annual World Bank data. Life expectancy, under-5 mortality and physicians per 1,000 are directional; health spending per capita and as a share of GDP are reported for comparison. Ranked values compare countries with each other.

verticals.title: Country education
verticals.question: How do these countries compare on education access and investment?
verticals.note: Annual World Bank data: secondary and tertiary gross enrollment and government education spending (% of GDP). China does not publish secondary enrollment to the World Bank. Ranked values compare countries with each other.

verticals.title: US Treasury yield curve
verticals.question: What shape is the Treasury curve, and is it inverting or steepening?
verticals.note: Higher score means a steeper curve than usual for the trailing year (10-year minus 3-month and minus 2-year spreads). term_structure gives every tenor and whether each slope is inverted (below zero) today; yields by tenor are watch items.

verticals.title: US bank health
verticals.question: Are bank failures or consumer complaints about banks rising?
verticals.note: Higher score means calmer than usual: fewer FDIC bank failures (quarterly, ten-year history) and fewer CFPB consumer complaints (monthly) than their own history. Complaints are unverified and grow with awareness, so read a low score with the drivers. Recent bank failures are listed under recent_events.

verticals.title: Euro area rates and major currencies
verticals.question: Where are ECB rates and the major currencies versus their history?
verticals.note: Higher score means easier euro area conditions than usual: lower ECB policy rates and euro short-term rate. Euro reference rates against the dollar, pound, yen, yuan and franc are watch items (how unusual today's rate is). Euro area HICP inflation is collected but left out until the ECB publishes it again: every ECB HICP series stops at December 2025 (new classification in 2026).
